summary: The note argues that climate change is a local issue, using the November 2023 "Storm Zephyr" mega-storm to show how extreme weather worsens pollution in one community. It describes sewage overflow, contaminated rivers, harm to birds and amphibians, and a spike in respiratory illness. It closes by calling for green infrastructure and community action.
one_line: Storm Zephyr's November 2023 strike shows how climate-driven extreme weather worsens local pollution, wildlife decline and health problems, and why infrastructure and community action are needed.
key_facts: Storm Zephyr, an unseasonable mega-storm, hit the community on November 5, 2023; its formation was attributed to warming ocean temperatures and it brought torrential rains and gale-force winds.

Sarah Jennings, director of the local Environmental Protection Agency, said at a November 8, 2023 press briefing that heavy rains overwhelmed sewage systems, forcing untreated waste into waterways and onto streets.
Floodwaters carried gasoline and oil from submerged vehicles and chemicals from inundated industrial sites into rivers and soil.
Local fisherman Michael Torres said on December 2, 2023: "The fish are gone, and all we're left with is the grime the storm left behind."
Biologist Dr. Emily Cheng said at a January 15, 2024 seminar that local bird populations were declining from habitat and food loss, since the insects they eat are highly sensitive to water quality.
Dr. Emily Cheng's research suggests native wetland amphibian populations are at dire risk from the pollutants Storm Zephyr introduced into their breeding grounds.
Public health official Dr. Robert Liu warned on February 27, 2024 that emergency room visits spiked after the storm, led by asthma and other respiratory issues linked to mold and particulates.
The CDC's March 1, 2024 report supported Dr. Liu's observations by linking climate change, extreme weather and rising pollution-related health issues nationwide.
Civil engineer Laura Gutierrez presented a proposal to the City Council on April 10, 2024 for green infrastructure such as rain gardens, permeable pavements and enhanced wetlands.
Educator Mark Stevenson launched a community clean-up initiative on September 22, 2023 that mobilizes residents to remove trash and debris from local waterways.

The note recommends individual actions such as reducing single-use plastics and environmentally conscious voting, alongside upgrading stormwater systems and reinforcing buildings against floods and wind.
